title: Too many good results
hook: meditation trials report more positive results than expected by chance (Coronado-Montoya et al., 2016)

segments.voice: Yesterday: what held up. Sleep, movement, other people, and practice, modestly. Your line was what held up. Did you do your small version? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

There's a drawer in this story. A researcher runs a careful trial of a meditation program. Months of work. The result comes back flat: no clear difference between the people who meditated and the people who didn't. It's honest, and it's dull, and it's hard to get anyone excited about printing it. So the paper goes into a drawer, and the researcher moves on. Nobody lied. Nobody cheated. Now multiply that drawer across a whole field. What reaches the public is the pile of studies that worked, and the pile looks wonderful. Today is about that pile, and about a team that counted it.
screen: `A CAREFUL TRIAL, A FLAT RESULT.` → `INTO THE DRAWER.` → `THE PILE THAT REACHES US.`

segments.voice: First, the question. A team led by Stephanie Coronado-Montoya looked at published trials of mindfulness-based therapies and asked something clever. Not, does it work? But, given how big these studies were, how many of them should we expect to come out positive, even if mindfulness really helps? Small studies miss real effects fairly often. So a healthy record should include some misses. Second, the answer. The published trials reported positive results far more often than their size would predict. Too many good results. That's the fingerprint of missing studies. Third, where the missing ones went. The team also checked trial registries, public lists where researchers announce a study before running it. A good share of registered trials had not been published long after they finished. The drawer, in other words, is real. Fourth, what this does and doesn't mean. It doesn't mean meditation does nothing. Yesterday's review still found modest benefits. It means the published picture is probably rosier than the full one, and the honest size of the effect is likely smaller than the brightest papers suggest. Paul, writing to the church at Thessalonica, put the posture plainly, in the King James text: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Test first. Then hold on. Not a cynic, who throws everything out, and not a fan, who keeps everything. Someone in the middle, with a question ready.
screen: `HOW MANY SHOULD COME OUT POSITIVE?` · `FAR MORE THAN EXPECTED.` · `THE DRAWER IS REAL.` · `ROSIER THAN THE FULL PICTURE.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a fair question. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think of one thing this path, or any app, book or teacher, has told you that practice will do for you. Calmer. Kinder. Sharper. Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold a bird. Ask two things. What would it look like if this weren't true for me? And what have I actually noticed? Let both answers be allowed. If you notice something real, keep it. If you notice nothing yet, keep sitting anyway, and keep asking. The bell holds the time.
Too many good results. When nearly every published trial is positive, some of the flat ones are probably in a drawer. Today's word.
Your line: a little sceptical. Today, when something promises a big change, ask where the flat results went. Test first, then hold on to what's good. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Researchers check for missing studies by comparing published trials with public trial registries and with how many positive results the studies' size would predict; researchers can also announce trials in public registries before running them.

fork.setup: you've run a careful meditation trial, and the result is flat. what do you do?
options: put it in a drawer and move on.
publish it anyway, flat result and all.
keep reanalyzing until something looks positive.
fork.reveal: publishing the flat result is what keeps the record honest. the drawer is what the team's counting suggests often happens instead.

trapdoor: what you thought: lots of positive studies means it really works.
what it means: if nearly every published trial is positive, some flat ones are probably missing, and the real effect is smaller.
what a scholar hears: Coronado-Montoya's team compared positive mindfulness trials with what the studies' size predicted, and checked trial registries.

sources.ref: Coronado-Montoya et al., "Reporting of positive results in randomized controlled trials of mindfulness-based mental health interventions" (PLOS ONE)

notes: The index carry 'a little sceptical' uses British spelling; the script keeps it exactly (the validator requires it) and avoids the word elsewhere. Owner may want to change the index to 'a little skeptical'.

Confirm the summary of Coronado-Montoya et al.: positive results in published mindfulness RCTs far exceeded the number expected from the trials' statistical power; of trials registered, a majority were unpublished long after completion. The voice says 'far more often' and 'a good share' and gives no numbers.

The drawer scene in the hook is illustrative (the 'file drawer' problem), not a specific case.
